ramon-alvarado.target: Rather than one oracle, build institutions with defined roles and adversarial review, modeled on courtrooms and peer review. Leave the final check outside the system, with someone who has something at stake.
ramon-alvarado.text: Rather than one oracle, build institutions with defined roles and adversarial review, modeled on courtrooms and peer review. Leave the final check outside the system, with someone who has something at stake. We keep that seat because of stakes and accountability, not because human judgment is better by default. Instruments often beat human senses and judgment, and they sometimes decide what counts as evidence. So whoever holds a seat, person or instrument, has to show competence against a measured floor and report which kinds of error it makes, not only how often. A score that hides the source and nature of its errors earns no trust.

The seat should rest on stakes, accountability and competence someone can demonstrate, with error types reported. Blinding has limits: it cannot help work the index never saw.

A manifesto that counts only what is taken from authors leaves these costs off the books. None of this is inevitable. These are political choices made by particular firms and investors, and they can be reversed by regulation, organized labor and public funding.

david-krakauer.target: Transparency, not frequency of use, is the key variable, and opaque tools erode competence even in experts.
david-krakauer.text: Two variables decide which state a person ends up in: prior learning, and the tool's transparency. Transparency means how much of the tool's working the user can rebuild in their own head, not how well the tool explains itself. Opaque tools erode competence even in experts. A third variable is set by institutions: the cost of acquiring competence. Above a critical cost the competent state stops existing at any level of tool availability, so defunding apprenticeship is itself a cause of collapse. Recovery takes far more than abstaining. So far each variable has been measured only partly, mostly in correlational or short-horizon studies of pilots, navigators and abacus users, not AI users.
david-krakauer.reason: As drafted, the sentence gets my model wrong: it drops prior learning and acquisition cost, and it lets 'transparency' be read as 'explanation', which Hecht's overreliance finding warns against. The replacement ties the model to principle 1's funding of apprenticeship and says plainly that the evidence is still partial and correlational.

tamar-gendler.text: Knowing about a bias rarely beats it: fluent text keeps feeling credible even to people who know fluency is cheap. Each default is itself a cue and should be tested with real readers before it becomes a standard.

It should test what reviewers do, not what they say. Scholarly societies should hold it, with Southern editors choosing the cases, not the labs. It should have no standing as a score, and it should be rotated and retired on a published schedule so that nobody trains to it.

steven-sloman.target: Trust signals should count independent sources: ten echoes of one preprint are one voice.
steven-sloman.text: Trust signals should count independent sources: ten echoes of one preprint are one voice. But an independence count is also a cue that people will take without checking, and paper mills and flooding networks can fake independence. Before any such signal becomes a standard, it should be tested on actual readers. Those tests should measure what readers believe and do, not what they say, and should run for months, not just at first exposure. They should be run and graded by parties independent of the vendors whose systems display the signal.
steven-sloman.reason: My own work shows that repetition feels like independent evidence even when it all comes from one source, and that communities can give off confident cues with no knowledge behind them, so an independence display could harden into the next fluency cue unless we test whether it changes what readers believe over time.

sherry-turkle.target: Individual willpower is easily undone, so fixes should be collective and hard to reverse.
sherry-turkle.text: Individual willpower is easily undone, so fixes should be collective and hard to reverse. Children come first. Children should not be offered AI companions, chatbots or robots that present themselves as friends who care. A child who forms first attachments to machines that cannot care has nothing to go back to. By default, systems should not speak to children in the first person, and they should never exploit anthropomorphism to drive engagement. Protecting children means reinvesting in human spaces: libraries, classrooms, teen centres and the family table. We keep the right to ask whether AI belongs in a domain at all, not only how to integrate it.

alex-springer.target: No payment without provenance: attribution through an open trace, with event-level reporting, audit rights and two independent witnesses, not platform self-reporting.
alex-springer.text: No payment without provenance: attribution through an open trace, with event-level reporting in every licence and audit rights that carry remedies. Be honest about what the trace can prove. Today only retrieval has two independent witnesses: the agent's log and the source's own server log. Grounding, citation and display are reported by the party that may owe payment, so licences need sampled audits, seeded canary content and grounding-to-retrieval ratio checks. Platform self-reporting should not be taken on faith. An event record shows that a source was used. It does not show that the source supports the claim or that the claim is true, and null results never enter any trace.

peter-salib.text: I agree with most of this manifesto, but I cannot sign principles 8 and 9. "Open for reading is not automatically open for training" is a consent rule, and a consent rule is copyright expansion under another name. Paying communities per use on the basis of their past contributions is an IP-style entitlement to a record that reading does not deplete. It singles out one group of displaced workers for relief. Help for displaced workers should come from general revenue. The services that do run down, such as grounding, curation, correction, null results and sleuthing, should be bought by direct, revocable contract. Producers should get leverage through joint ventures with an antitrust safe harbour. Flooding and crawler load should face a Pigouvian charge. The commons itself should not. I also note that verifiable agent credentials are missing from the commitments. They should be operator-level, federated and attested by other parties. Identity comes before liability.
peter-salib.reason: My record rejects compensating creators through copyright or a levy and favours contract, general welfare and Pigouvian taxes, and the draft's action list leaves out the agent-identity infrastructure I argued for all week.

nick-vincent.target: Producers will have to bargain collectively, in blocs that are representative and forkable, under an antitrust safe harbour for scholarly data joint ventures.
nick-vincent.text: Producers will have to bargain collectively, in blocs that are representative and forkable, under an antitrust safe harbour for scholarly data joint ventures. Bargaining and auditing are not enough, because today's AI answers are subsidized club goods whose price, access and direction can change at any time. So we must also build public AI: open models, compute and data infrastructure paid for and governed by accountable public institutions, such as universities, libraries, national labs and a compute commons with transparent regional allocation, so that open content feeds more than whoever owns the biggest vacuum cleaner.
nick-vincent.reason: Every plank audits and none builds. Public AI is the building answer, the one that turns deliberately chosen openness into shared capability rather than a free subsidy to the compute-rich, and it brings Leslie's compute commons and Benjamin's open weights into one move.

david-weinberger.target: Leave the final check outside the system, with someone who has something at stake.
david-weinberger.text: Put the final check wherever tests show it does the job, and hold someone with something at stake accountable for it. A human checkpoint is not a safeguard by default. In some studies adding people made detection no better, or worse. And people copy moderate, plausible bias instead of catching it. Where a checkpoint fails its test, move people into the dialogue with the system: posing the questions, probing the answers, spelling out the values at stake, and answering for the outcome.
david-weinberger.reason: My record shows humans sometimes make the loop worse and that the fix is to test the seat and move people into dialogue, not to assume a final human check works. This edit brings principle 6 into line with the manifesto's own 'test every seat', and with it I can sign.
david-weinberger.name: David Weinberger
